title: Hedging, stance and cautious claims
objectives: Form common modal and appears-to patterns.
Select a level of certainty appropriate to stated evidence.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A hedge limits the force or scope of a claim. It can show uncertainty, identify a tendency rather than a universal rule, or signal that a conclusion is based on incomplete evidence. “The change may reduce costs” presents a possibility; “The change reduces costs” presents a more direct claim. Neither wording is automatically better: the choice should match what the writer knows.

Hedging is common in research, professional discussion and polite disagreement. It can prevent a claim from going beyond the evidence. It can also make a recommendation less abrupt: “It might be useful to check the figures” is less direct than “Check the figures”. The listener still needs enough information to understand the recommendation.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Modal verbs such as may, might and could can express possibility. Adverbs such as generally, often and apparently can qualify frequency or source, but they are not interchangeable: “generally” concerns a broad pattern, while “apparently” signals how something seems or is reported. Expressions such as “appears to” and “seems to” present an interpretation without asserting it in the most direct way.

A quantifier can also narrow scope. “Some participants reported a delay” does not imply that all participants did. “Most participants reported a delay” claims a majority; it is stronger than some in ordinary use. An accurate percentage is often clearer than either expression when reliable figures are available.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare “The survey proves that the policy works” with “The survey suggests that the policy may work.” The second sentence treats the results as evidence for a possible conclusion rather than as conclusive proof. It is suitable only if that degree of uncertainty reflects the evidence; the writer should not weaken a well-established fact merely to sound academic.

In a meeting, “There may be a problem with the schedule” opens the issue without claiming certainty. “The schedule is wrong” may be appropriate after the team has verified an error. In both cases, a precise explanation of the evidence helps the listener assess the statement.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not treat all hedges as synonyms. “The results generally improved” states a broad pattern; “The results possibly improved” questions whether improvement occurred. The position of a hedge also matters: “Some students may pass” leaves open which and how many, while “Most students may pass” predicts a possible majority.

Avoid stacking several vague expressions when one would communicate the intended stance: “It may possibly perhaps be useful” is grammatically possible but often unnecessarily weak and awkward. Distinguish uncertainty from politeness and from limited frequency. Choose the device whose meaning matches the actual claim.

examples.note: Generally describes a broad pattern, not an absolute rule.
Some limits the claim to an unspecified part of the group.
Most claims a majority in ordinary use.

examples.sentence: The figures appear to support the proposal.
examples.note: Appear to marks an interpretation of the figures.

examples.sentence: It might be useful to check the figures.
examples.note: Might makes the suggestion less direct.

examples.sentence: The schedule is wrong; the verified dates do not match.
examples.note: A direct claim can be appropriate when supported by evidence.
Apparently signals how the information seems or is reported.

common_errors.incorrect: The figures may supports the proposal.
common_errors.correct: The figures may support the proposal.
common_errors.reason: May takes the base form support.

common_errors.correct: The policy appears to reduce costs.
common_errors.reason: Appears takes a to-infinitive in this pattern.
Use plural participants for an unspecified group of countable people here.

summary: Hedges qualify certainty, frequency or scope in different ways.
Choose the strength of a claim to match the evidence.
Use precise qualifiers and avoid unnecessary stacking.

exercises.prompt: Choose a possible effect, not a definite result.
exercises.explanation: May presents the reduction as possible.

options.text: The change has certainly reduced costs.
The change did reduce costs yesterday.

option_feedback.a: “The change reduces costs.” does not fit here. May presents the reduction as possible.
option_feedback.b: “The change has certainly reduced costs.” does not fit here. May presents the reduction as possible.
option_feedback.c: “The change did reduce costs yesterday.” does not fit here. May presents the reduction as possible.
option_feedback.d: “The change may reduce costs.” fits here. May presents the reduction as possible.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence reports a broad tendency?
exercises.explanation: Generally qualifies the frequency or overall pattern.

options.text: The results did not ever improve.

option_feedback.a: “The results generally improved.” fits here. Generally qualifies the frequency or overall pattern.
option_feedback.b: “The results possibly improved.” does not fit here. Generally qualifies the frequency or overall pattern.
option_feedback.c: “The results cannot improve.” does not fit here. Generally qualifies the frequency or overall pattern.
option_feedback.d: “The results did not ever improve.” does not fit here. Generally qualifies the frequency or overall pattern.

exercises.prompt: Which expression refers to a majority in ordinary use?
exercises.explanation: Most participants refers to more than half in ordinary use.

option_feedback.a: “no participants” does not fit here. Most participants refers to more than half in ordinary use.
option_feedback.b: “one participant” does not fit here. Most participants refers to more than half in ordinary use.
option_feedback.c: “most participants” fits here. Most participants refers to more than half in ordinary use.
option_feedback.d: “neither participant” does not fit here. Most participants refers to more than half in ordinary use.

exercises.prompt: Choose the grammatical hedged claim.
exercises.explanation: May is followed by the base form reduce.

options.text: The plan may to reduce costs.

option_feedback.a: “The plan may reduces costs.” does not fit here. May is followed by the base form reduce.
option_feedback.b: “The plan may reduce costs.” fits here. May is followed by the base form reduce.
option_feedback.c: “The plan may to reduce costs.” does not fit here. May is followed by the base form reduce.
option_feedback.d: “The plan may reducing costs.” does not fit here. May is followed by the base form reduce.

exercises.prompt: Complete the interpretation: The figures appear ___ the proposal.
exercises.explanation: Appear is followed by a to-infinitive here.

option_feedback.a: “support” does not fit here. Appear is followed by a to-infinitive here.
option_feedback.b: “supporting to” does not fit here. Appear is followed by a to-infinitive here.
option_feedback.c: “to support” fits here. Appear is followed by a to-infinitive here.
option_feedback.d: “supports” does not fit here. Appear is followed by a to-infinitive here.

exercises.prompt: Which is a less direct suggestion?
exercises.explanation: Might be useful presents the suggestion tentatively.

options.text: It might be useful to check the figures.

option_feedback.a: “It might be useful to check the figures.” fits here. Might be useful presents the suggestion tentatively.
option_feedback.b: “Check the figures now!” does not fit here. Might be useful presents the suggestion tentatively.
option_feedback.c: “The figures were checked.” does not fit here. Might be useful presents the suggestion tentatively.
option_feedback.d: “The figures are definitely wrong.” does not fit here. Might be useful presents the suggestion tentatively.

exercises.prompt: What does “Some participants reported delays” establish?
exercises.explanation: Some limits the statement without identifying the entire group.

options.text: An unspecified part of the group reported delays.
The delays were proven to affect everyone.

option_feedback.a: “All participants reported delays.” does not fit here. Some limits the statement without identifying the entire group.
option_feedback.b: “An unspecified part of the group reported delays.” fits here. Some limits the statement without identifying the entire group.
option_feedback.c: “No participants reported delays.” does not fit here. Some limits the statement without identifying the entire group.
option_feedback.d: “The delays were proven to affect everyone.” does not fit here. Some limits the statement without identifying the entire group.

exercises.prompt: Which practice improves precision?
exercises.explanation: Different qualifiers express different kinds and degrees of limitation.

options.text: Use may perhaps possibly in every sentence.
Replace all figures with vague language.
Treat apparently and generally as identical.
Match the qualifier to the evidence and intended meaning.

option_feedback.a: “Use may perhaps possibly in every sentence.” does not fit here. Different qualifiers express different kinds and degrees of limitation.
option_feedback.b: “Replace all figures with vague language.” does not fit here. Different qualifiers express different kinds and degrees of limitation.
option_feedback.c: “Treat apparently and generally as identical.” does not fit here. Different qualifiers express different kinds and degrees of limitation.
option_feedback.d: “Match the qualifier to the evidence and intended meaning.” fits here. Different qualifiers express different kinds and degrees of limitation.
